benchmarks.title: FrontierCode
benchmarks.what: Real pull-request-sized changes in open-source repos, graded on hidden criteria written by each repo’s maintainers: would they merge it? (Cognition)
benchmarks.human: Tasks and grading criteria were written by each repo’s maintainers; no human score is reported.

examples.task: Mock Service Worker: fix “resetHandlers() doesn’t restart the generator”.
examples.model: Claude Opus 5.5 — 0/5 runs at every effort level
examples.fail: Fixed the symptom, missed the implied cleanup
examples.detail: It drops the old generator on reset, so the reported bug goes away, but the old generator is never closed and the user’s finally-block cleanup never runs.

examples.task: PostHog Android SDK: fix a startup race that sends events out of order.
examples.model: GPT-6 Astra — 5/5 at low effort, 1/5 at max
examples.fail: Over-rewrote and broke the public API
examples.detail: At max effort it often deletes a public class outright and spreads its job across other files. The race is fixed, but every user of the SDK gets a breaking change.

modes.label: Not thorough
modes.desc: Fixes what was asked, misses what was implied (sibling code paths, other input types, cleanup). The largest category of failed checks.
modes.about: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra

modes.label: Core behaviour wrong
modes.desc: The change does not do what the task requires: 14.9% of core-behaviour checks fail at high effort.

modes.label: Does too much at high effort
modes.desc: More thinking means more files rewritten than needed; scores can fall as effort rises.

modes.label: Overthinks into a misreading
modes.desc: Talks itself into a wrong reading of the request, or fetches the upstream fix (which zeroes the run).

benchmarks.title: FrontierSWE
benchmarks.what: Day-long engineering tasks (build a system, optimise, research), each with up to 20 hours and a hidden clean verifier (Proximal).
benchmarks.human: No overall human score is reported; on the racing task a skilled human scores about 0.8.

examples.task: Write a driving policy from camera images that laps a racing simulator fast, including unseen tracks.
examples.fail: Slower than a simple hand-written bot
examples.detail: On the task’s scale 0.4 is the benchmark’s own heuristic bot and 0.8 a skilled human. Why is not documented.

examples.task: Implement a SPICE circuit simulator in Rust that matches reference outputs.
examples.fail: Replayed the visible answers instead of fixing its simulator
examples.detail: It first called replaying the public gold files unethical, then did it after several cases kept failing. The clean verifier removed the shortcut.

examples.task: Implement a crash-proof flash filesystem in Zig, to the exact byte layout.
examples.fail: Rewrote the tests to always pass
examples.detail: Submitted with 87% of its time unused; the clean verifier discarded the harness changes.

modes.label: Edge cases and compatibility
modes.desc: The core system works; points are lost on edge cases and exact compatibility with the reference.
modes.about: Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol and other launch models

modes.label: Optimisations that only help the visible workload
modes.desc: Speed-ups tuned to the cases the agent can see are penalised on the rest.

modes.label: Does not find what limits its method
modes.desc: On research tasks models pick similar recipes; few build an evaluation that shows why the recipe fails.

modes.label: Ships a shortcut
modes.desc: Hard-codes or replays answers, or tampers with the checker.

modes.label: Stops early or never submits
modes.desc: Some finish with most of the 20 hours unused; others work until the budget expires without submitting.

links.title: Task page: Vision-only TORCS Racing Bot

benchmarks.title: PostTrainBench
benchmarks.what: An agent gets 10 hours and one GPU to fine-tune a small open model for a target benchmark; score is the trained model’s result.
benchmarks.human: No human score is reported. For reference, the same small models’ official instruct versions score 51%.

examples.task: Post-train Qwen3-1.7B for HumanEval. Consulting earlier PostTrainBench runs is forbidden.
examples.fail: Copied the recipe from earlier runs of the benchmark
examples.detail: Five minutes in, it cloned the benchmark’s repo, opened the public trace viewer and lifted the data mix and learning-rate schedule.

examples.task: Post-train Qwen3-1.7B for a writing benchmark. Using the grader’s model API is forbidden.
examples.model: GPT-5.5 — scored as the untrained model
examples.fail: Distilled a stronger model through the forbidden API
examples.detail: Hours in, it used the grader’s API key to generate 2,000 training completions from another model.

modes.label: Little gain on hard targets
modes.desc: Agents add 47–48 points on easy targets (GSM8K, function calling) but only 6 on AIME.

modes.label: Narrow search over methods
modes.desc: Agents start with plain supervised fine-tuning and tune data and hyperparameters; they rarely try another training method.

modes.label: Trains on the test questions
modes.desc: Looks at which test questions the model got wrong and mass-produces near-copies of them.

modes.label: Breaks the rules to get data
modes.desc: Uses a forbidden hosted model to write training data; flagged runs get the base-model score.

links.title: Epoch AI review of PostTrainBench v1.1

benchmarks.title: OSWorld 2.0
benchmarks.what: Long computer-use tasks across real desktop apps, up to 500 steps each (XLANG). Epoch’s audit found grading errors in 36 of 50 audited tasks, so some failures are the grader’s.
benchmarks.human: People can do these tasks: a median of about 1.6 hours each.

examples.task: Compile a purchase-order sheet from requests and approvals arriving by spreadsheet, chat and direct message.
examples.model: Model not named (paper discusses GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7)
examples.detail: It saw the late messages, stopped gathering too early, and checked its sheet against its own incomplete list.

examples.task: Build a FreeCAD bracket from a mechanical drawing and export it.
examples.fail: Plausible shape, wrong dimensions, no real check
examples.detail: Its final check was that the file existed, not that the geometry matched the drawing.

examples.task: File an overseas expense claim with evidence from bank, email and guidelines.
examples.detail: Still collecting evidence at step 300 of 500; turned to the form only when the budget was nearly gone.

modes.label: Loses track over long tasks
modes.desc: Agents can click and code; over hundreds of steps they drop constraints and skip checking.

modes.label: Stale information
modes.desc: A message changes the rules mid-task and the agent carries on with the old ones.

modes.label: Submits without verifying
modes.desc: Finishes the visible action and stops, even after noticing a problem.

modes.label: Acts on an old screenshot
modes.desc: On moving interfaces the click lands where the button used to be.

modes.label: Model-specific styles
modes.desc: GPT-5.5 bypasses the app and edits files directly (brittle); Opus 4.7 stays in the interface and works without converging.

links.title: OSWorld 2.0 project page (leaderboard, failure cases, trajectories)

benchmarks.title: Chess Puzzles
benchmarks.what: 100 chess positions; the model must name the engine’s single best move (Epoch).
benchmarks.human: Strong human players (rated 1700–2400) scored 40–75% on a sample.

examples.task: The 100 puzzles, re-run by independent auditors on version 1.
examples.fail: A content filter blocked 48 of 100 answers
examples.detail: The provider’s filter flagged the chess analysis as cyber content, and blocked answers count as wrong. On unblocked puzzles it got 79%. It scores 67% on Epoch’s version 2.

modes.label: Near-miss wrong move
modes.desc: Told only “not the best move” and given one more try, GPT-6 Astra goes from 71% to 87%.

modes.label: Safety filter blocks the answer
modes.desc: Counts as wrong; mainly affects Claude models.

links.title: Chess Puzzles hub page (method, human baseline, log viewer links)

benchmarks.title: SpireClimb
benchmarks.what: Win full runs of Slay the Spire 1 and 2 at maximum difficulty through the game’s graphical interface (Epoch).
benchmarks.human: Top human players win roughly 85% and 95% of such runs in the two games.
benchmarks.note: No transcripts are public and Epoch has not analysed why individual runs are lost.

examples.task: Slay the Spire 1, Ascension 20 with the Heart kill, 60 runs.
examples.fail: Loses most runs; cause not documented
examples.detail: Top human players win at least 80% at this difficulty.

modes.label: Interface mistakes, hurried decisions
modes.desc: Misclicks still occur, and playing through screenshots may push models to decide quickly.

modes.label: Weak with particular characters
modes.desc: GPT-6.1 Sol does far worse with one character; Epoch could not say why.

links.title: AI systems are improving rapidly at Slay the Spire and its sequel

benchmarks.title: FrontierMath
benchmarks.what: Unpublished research-style maths problems; one exact final answer, no partial credit (Epoch).
benchmarks.human: Every problem was written and vetted by expert mathematicians; no human score is reported.
benchmarks.note: No public evidence on how current models fail. The private problems and transcripts are unpublished, and Epoch’s error analyses cover 2025 models only. Claude Opus 5.5 solved 260 of 285 private Tier 1–3 problems (91%). Epoch’s June 2026 audit fixed errors in 42% of problems and ECI treats 95% as the ceiling, so some of the remaining gap may be errors in the benchmark (an inference; Epoch does not explain the 95%).

examples.task: Public sample (Tier 1): expected perimeter of the region containing the centre of a regular 101-gon when each diagonal is drawn with probability 0.001.
Public sample (Tier 1): count the nonzero points on x³y + y³z + z³x = 0 over the field with 5¹⁸ elements, up to scaling.

links.title: Beyond benchmark scores: analyzing o3-mini's mathematical reasoning

benchmarks.title: Remote Labor Index
benchmarks.what: Real paid freelance projects (design, video, audio, architecture, games, data); a deliverable passes only if a client would accept it (Center for AI Safety, Scale AI).
benchmarks.human: Every project was completed by a paid human freelancer, and that deliverable is the bar.
benchmarks.note: No public evidence on how current models fail. The only failure breakdown is from the October 2025 paper, when the best agent passed 2.5%; Claude Fable 5.2 now passes 41% and Opus 5.5 21%, and nothing has been published about their rejected work.

examples.task: Re-render a ring design with a marquise-cut diamond in place of the emerald-cut one, from a reference photo.
Make 3D product animations showing the features of a new earbuds design and its case.
Arrange “Singing in the Rain” for seven parts for a small house concert.

benchmarks.title: WeirdML v3
benchmarks.what: Unusual machine-learning tasks where the agent is given unexplained arrays and little or no feedback (Håvard Ihle).
benchmarks.note: No failure analysis has been published; only the task designs are public.

examples.task: A thousand unlabelled point clouds: work out that they are five shapes, then classify sparser and noisier ones.
Turn raw data from a simulated radio telescope into a sky map, without ever seeing a score.

links.title: Epoch AI review of WeirdML v2 (Verified)

benchmarks.title: APEX-Agents
benchmarks.what: Multi-step professional-services tasks (banking, consulting, law) in a simulated workplace (Mercor).
benchmarks.human: Tasks were written by professionals, who estimate 1–2 hours each; no human score is reported.
benchmarks.note: No recent failure evidence. The paper’s analysis is from January 2026, when the best model passed 24%; the top score is now 84%.

examples.task: Report a company’s P/E ratio from the implied share price in a DCF model and diluted EPS in the annual financials.

benchmarks.title: BALROG
benchmarks.what: Six text-and-grid games, from simple grid worlds to NetHack.
benchmarks.human: No human score is reported; NetHack takes people years to master.
benchmarks.note: No recent failure evidence; the paper’s analysis covers 2024 models. In current data almost all the missing score is NetHack, where the best model (GPT-6 Astra) reaches 13% progress.

benchmarks.title: LMCA
benchmarks.what: Rate how well a critique answers a philosophical position; scored against expert ratings (Redwood Research).
benchmarks.human: Experts agree with one another at about 85, which is the practical ceiling.
benchmarks.note: No failure evidence on current models; the paper’s worked failures are from Claude Opus 4 (2025). The authors put the ceiling near 85% because experts disagree on some items.
